did_you_know.text: Deuteronomy states that Moses lived to be 120. Later it adds that even at that age his eyes had not dimmed and his strength had not faded.
The name Joshua is related to the Hebrew root y-sh-ʿ, meaning rescue or salvation. His name therefore suits his role as the leader who will guide the people.
The gathering described here is traditionally called Hakhel. It took place at Sukkot after the sabbatical year, once every seven years.
The word ger here refers to a foreign resident living among the Israelites, not only to someone who converted. That person, too, was included among those who learned.
Ohel Moed is the biblical name for the Tabernacle, where sacred service took place and divine revelation was described. Its name means “Tent of Meeting.”
“This song” is the Song of Moses, found in the next chapter, Deuteronomy 32. A song can help people remember important ideas and pass them from one generation to the next.

In societies where much knowledge was passed on orally, a song was an especially useful memory tool: rhythm and repetition helped preserve its words. That is why the song could serve as a witness in the future.
The biblical phrase “ad tumam” means “until it was fully completed.” It refers not merely to finishing a sentence, but to completing the entire writing.

Calling heaven and earth as witnesses is covenant language: the whole world is pictured as present and able to testify to the people’s choices. A similar idea appears in Deuteronomy chapters 4 and 30.
The chapter ends with a song, and the next chapter immediately continues with the Song of Moses. In this way, the Torah connects a spoken message with one preserved in poetic form.
